report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Emotion is rooted in bodily physiology and socially constructed through language and culture.
We propose the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via Collective Predictive Coding, integrating interoception into agents' generative models within an active-inference framework.

Emotion emerges through coupled loops of individual allostatic regulation and social communication: bodily evidence grounds shared emotion words, while negotiated words shape bodily inference and regulation.

This framework bridges psychological and social constructivism, aligns with findings on emotional contagion and concept formation, and supports constructive verification in multi-agent robotic systems.
It also offers a computational account of alexithymia as a disconnection between interoception and social symbols, linking individual embodiment with evolving social symbol systems.
Our emotions are inextricably dual: psychologically constructed and rooted in the body, while simultaneously socially constructed and rooted in language and culture.
Language, culture, and their value systems are often treated as static givens.
Yet the term "social construction" itself signals otherwise: they are continuously co-produced by the agents who use them.
In this sense, emotions are co-constructed.
Despite the emphasis on social construction in constructivist theories of emotion, the bottom-up pathways involved in this process have not been sufficiently theorized.

Although current constructivist frameworks acknowledge reciprocal relations between bodily experience and social meaning, they have mostly formalized how "already constructed" language, culture, and norms exert a top-down influence on our emotions.
This perspective remains incomplete.
Indeed, Parkinson (2012) argues that the social construction of emotion is no longer in question, and that the outstanding task is to specify how these processes operate and what materials they use.
text.formatted: Indeed, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Parkinson (2012)</ref> argues that the social construction of emotion is no longer in question, and that the outstanding task is to specify how these processes operate and what materials they use.

text.text: A bottom-up computational account is precisely positioned to answer this call for mechanism.
In this paper, we build on Collective Predictive Coding (CPC) (Taniguchi, 2024a) and Collective Active Inference (CAIF) (Taniguchi et al., 2026) to present a novel theoretical framework.
text.formatted: In this paper, we build on Collective Predictive Coding (CPC) <ref type="bibr">(Taniguchi, 2024a)</ref> and Collective Active Inference (CAIF) <ref type="bibr">(Taniguchi et al., 2026)</ref> to present a novel theoretical framework.

text.text: We describe how people, through interaction, actively form emotion words and associated linguistic systems within a community, or semiosphere.
These emergent systems, in turn, shape individuals' emotional understanding and bodily regulation.

Barrett's Theory of Constructed Emotion (TCE) (Barrett, 2017a (Barrett, , 2017b;; Barrett & Miller, 2026) has driven a paradigm shift in emotion research by redefining emotion not as a passive reaction to external stimuli, but as an active predictive process in which the brain constructs meaning from interoceptive fluctuations (Barrett & Simmons, 2015).
text.formatted: Barrett's Theory of Constructed Emotion (TCE) <ref type="bibr">(Barrett, 2017a</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Barrett, , 2017b;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Barrett & Miller, 2026)</ref> has driven a paradigm shift in emotion research by redefining emotion not as a passive reaction to external stimuli, but as an active predictive process in which the brain constructs meaning from interoceptive fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Barrett & Simmons, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In this view, the brain mobilizes prior concepts to infer the causes of uncertain bodily signals, thereby constructing emotional episodes suited to the current context.

However, even this sophisticated framework typically treats the generative mechanisms by which emotional concepts and linguistic categories themselves are formed and shared as given: society and culture appear only as fixed top-down priors on individual processing, and their bottom-up co-construction is left unaddressed.
Social constructivism (Harré, 1986; Reddy, 2001) has long emphasized that emotions are shaped by historical and cultural discourse.
text.formatted: Social constructivism <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Harré, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Reddy, 2001)</ref> has long emphasized that emotions are shaped by historical and cultural discourse.

text.text: Interoceptive accounts (Craig, 2002; Seth, 2013; Seth & Friston, 2016) use the Free Energy Principle (FEP) (K. Friston, 2010) and active inference (AIF) (Parr et al., 2022) to show how socially shared concepts function as top-down priors that regulate interoceptive prediction error, vividly demonstrating the link between social meaning and individual bodily experience.
text.formatted: Interoceptive accounts <ref type="bibr">(Craig, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Seth, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seth & Friston, 2016)</ref> use the Free Energy Principle (FEP) (K. <ref type="bibr">Friston, 2010)</ref> and active inference (AIF) <ref type="bibr">(Parr et al., 2022)</ref> to show how socially shared concepts function as top-down priors that regulate interoceptive prediction error, vividly demonstrating the link between social meaning and individual bodily experience.

text.text: Yet even in these models, language and society serve as fixed environments external to the agent.

What remains unaddressed is the cyclical process of co-construction itself (Ohira, 2020a): how the social predictive model that regulates individual emotion emerges bottom-up from affective interactions and continues to dynamically evolve.
text.formatted: What remains unaddressed is the cyclical process of co-construction itself <ref type="bibr">(Ohira, 2020a)</ref>: how the social predictive model that regulates individual emotion emerges bottom-up from affective interactions and continues to dynamically evolve.

text.text: Symbol Emergence in Robotics (Taniguchi et al., 2016 (Taniguchi et al., , 2018)), a constructive approach to symbol emergence systems and developing minds, offers a constructive answer to this challenge: it reframes language not as a predefined symbolic system, but as a dynamic system that self-organizes bottom-up through physical and social interactions among agents.
text.formatted: Symbol Emergence in Robotics <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Taniguchi et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Taniguchi et al., , 2018))</ref>, a constructive approach to symbol emergence systems and developing minds, offers a constructive answer to this challenge: it reframes language not as a predefined symbolic system, but as a dynamic system that self-organizes bottom-up through physical and social interactions among agents.

text.text: CPC (Taniguchi, 2024a) formalizes this symbol emergence as decentralized Bayesian inference and extends FEP (K. Friston, 2010 Friston, , 2019) ) to the social level.
text.formatted: CPC <ref type="bibr">(Taniguchi, 2024a)</ref> formalizes this symbol emergence as decentralized Bayesian inference and extends FEP (K. <ref type="bibr">Friston, 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Friston, , 2019) )</ref> to the social level.

text.text: Building on CPC, we extend symbol emergence to the domain of emotion and propose the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via CPC, which integrates it with active inference by incorporating interoception into each agent's generative model, alongside exteroception, internal and external representations, and symbolic information.

Individual interoceptive regulation and social concept sharing thus become processes driven by the same mathematical principle: an internal loop of allostasis regulates individual bodily states, and a social loop of communication shares emotional concepts.
Bodily experience grounds the negotiation of shared symbols, while those symbols shape individual bodily prediction and regulation.

The unique contribution of this study is the explicit incorporation of interoception (Barrett & Simmons, 2015; Craig, 2002; Seth, 2013) into the conventional CPC framework, which has primarily focused on exteroceptive symbol sharing.
text.formatted: The unique contribution of this study is the explicit incorporation of interoception <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Barrett & Simmons, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Craig, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Seth, 2013)</ref> into the conventional CPC framework, which has primarily focused on exteroceptive symbol sharing.

text.text: This extension is non-trivial because interoceptive states are private, low-resolution, and only indirectly accessible, whereas CPC has typically modeled symbol sharing through externally observable signals.
Grounding this extension in FEP connects individual bodily inference and regulation to the collective perspective of CAIF.

Consequently, our model extends beyond mere passive shared perception to encompass bodily regulation aimed at minimizing interoceptive prediction errors-namely, mechanisms of homeostasis and allostasis-within the context of collective interaction.

This extension makes it possible, for the first time, to describe within a single mathematical framework the dynamic process by which "private bodily sensations" and "public symbols" mutually constrain and co-construct one another.
The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows: 1.

Theoretical Integration: We propose TCoE via CPC, which unifies the bodily and social construction of emotion within a single mathematical framework, computationally bridging individual interoceptive processes and social symbolic processes.

Clinical Implications: We redefine alexithymia computationally as a failure of emotional co-construction-a disconnection between interoception and social symbols-offering a novel interpretation through the lens of predictive processing.

We show that TCoE provides a foundation verifiable through constructive experiments using multi-agent robotic systems and artificial intelligence (AI), opening a new frontier between computational neuroscience and robotics.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 reviews psychological and neuroscientific evidence, Section 3 examines constructive models of embodied emotion, and Section 4 presents TCoE via CPC.
Section 5 offers a computational account of alexithymia, Section 6 discusses empirical predictions, and Section 7 concludes.
2 Empirical Foundations: Psychological and Neuroscientific Evidence
Predictive coding treats perception as inference through generative models, rather than passive registration of sensory input (K. Friston, 2010; Rao & Ballard, 1999).
text.formatted: Predictive coding treats perception as inference through generative models, rather than passive registration of sensory input (K. <ref type="bibr">Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Rao & Ballard, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to interoception, it concerns how bodily signals are interpreted and connected to regulation (Craig, 2002 (Craig, , 2009;; Seth, 2013).
text.formatted: Applied to interoception, it concerns how bodily signals are interpreted and connected to regulation <ref type="bibr">(Craig, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Craig, , 2009;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Seth, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This provides a framework for relating physiological fluctuations to emotional experience without assuming that a bodily pattern uniquely specifies an emotion.
Predictive processing has also been proposed as an integrative account of perception, action, affect, and subjective experience (Ohira, 2023).
text.formatted: Predictive processing has also been proposed as an integrative account of perception, action, affect, and subjective experience <ref type="bibr">(Ohira, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Interoceptive inference connects expectations about bodily conditions to autonomic, endocrine, and immune regulation (Seth, 2013; Seth & Friston, 2016).
text.formatted: Interoceptive inference connects expectations about bodily conditions to autonomic, endocrine, and immune regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">(Seth, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seth & Friston, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Allostasis emphasizes anticipated bodily needs rather than only correction of an existing deviation (Sterling, 2012).
text.formatted: Allostasis emphasizes anticipated bodily needs rather than only correction of an existing deviation <ref type="bibr">(Sterling, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Barrett's body-budget account places predictive resource regulation at the center of constructed emo-tion (Barrett, 2017a).
text.formatted: Barrett's body-budget account places predictive resource regulation at the center of constructed emo-tion <ref type="bibr">(Barrett, 2017a)</ref>.

text.text: The related allostasis-first perspective treats mental phenomena as developing from the coordination of physiological resources (Theriault et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The related allostasis-first perspective treats mental phenomena as developing from the coordination of physiological resources <ref type="bibr">(Theriault et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Large-scale neuroimaging supports an allostatic-interoceptive account of brain function.

Using the Embodied Predictive Interoception Coding (EPIC) model, Kleckner and colleagues identified a distributed system involving insular, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal regions, linking its connectivity to interoceptive ability (Kleckner et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Using the Embodied Predictive Interoception Coding (EPIC) model, Kleckner and colleagues identified a distributed system involving insular, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal regions, linking its connectivity to interoceptive ability <ref type="bibr">(Kleckner et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Connectivity studies further describe gradients related to allostatic and interoceptive functions across cortical and subcortical structures (Katsumi et al., 2022 (Katsumi et al., , 2023;; J. Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Connectivity studies further describe gradients related to allostatic and interoceptive functions across cortical and subcortical structures <ref type="bibr">(Katsumi et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Katsumi et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">J. Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support the view that interoceptive predictive processing contributes broadly to emotion, decision-making, and cognitive control.
Because allostatic regulation acts on expectations about forthcoming bodily demands, contexts and acquired concepts can shape those expectations.
TCoE extends this point to how the symbols entering such expectations are socially formed and revised.
Direct evidence for interoceptive predictive coding remains limited, but converging findings support the account.

Human studies show that anterior insular and anterior cingulate activity covaries with interoceptive attention and autonomic arousal, establishing these regions as key neural substrates of body-state representation (Craig, 2009; Critchley et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Human studies show that anterior insular and anterior cingulate activity covaries with interoceptive attention and autonomic arousal, establishing these regions as key neural substrates of body-state representation <ref type="bibr">(Craig, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Critchley et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Animal studies provide complementary evidence about anticipated bodily conditions.
In hungry or thirsty mice, cues associated with food or water shift insular activity toward patterns related to future satiety (Livneh et al., 2020; Namboodiri & Stuber, 2020).
text.formatted: In hungry or thirsty mice, cues associated with food or water shift insular activity toward patterns related to future satiety <ref type="bibr">(Livneh et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Namboodiri & Stuber, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This links insular representations to anticipated as well as current physiological states and motivates examining how learned contextual cues enter bodily regulation.
Immune regulation provides another example.

Koren and colleagues identified insular neuronal ensembles active during colitis or peritonitis in mice; chemogenetic reactivation sub-sequently reinstated corresponding inflammatory responses (Koren et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Koren and colleagues identified insular neuronal ensembles active during colitis or peritonitis in mice; chemogenetic reactivation sub-sequently reinstated corresponding inflammatory responses <ref type="bibr">(Koren et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The authors interpreted this as immune memory.

For an interoceptive predictive account, however, the important observation is that reactivating a neural representation can reproduce a peripheral bodily response, rather than merely recalling information.
We interpret this as consistent with reinstated predictions recruiting bodily responses to reduce prediction error, even when the resulting inflammation is harmful (Koren et al., 2021; Rolls, 2023).
text.formatted: We interpret this as consistent with reinstated predictions recruiting bodily responses to reduce prediction error, even when the resulting inflammation is harmful <ref type="bibr">(Koren et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rolls, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This supports a predictive-processing interpretation in which reducing a mismatch need not benefit the body.
Recent glucose-regulation experiments provide further support for anticipatory control.
Litvak and colleagues report that insular activity shifts toward a future metabolic-state representation before meal onset.
Suppressing anticipatory insular activity impaired anticipatory insulin release and subsequent metabolic homeostasis (Litvak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Suppressing anticipatory insular activity impaired anticipatory insulin release and subsequent metabolic homeostasis <ref type="bibr">(Litvak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings support a feedforward contribution of insular predictions to bodily regulation, consistent with interoceptive predictive coding.
Supplementary Section S3 retains procedural details and the extended empirical discussion.
Homeostatic reinforcement learning (HRL) grounds reward in the reduction of deviations from physiologically desirable states (Hulme et al., 2019; Keramati & Gutkin, 2014; Pezzulo et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Homeostatic reinforcement learning (HRL) grounds reward in the reduction of deviations from physiologically desirable states <ref type="bibr">(Hulme et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Keramati & Gutkin, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pezzulo et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It therefore connects motivation and action selection to internal bodily needs rather than treating external rewards as the sole source of value.
This makes HRL relevant to constructive accounts in which emotion depends on regulation of an embodied agent.
A related proposal links emotional valence to changes in prediction error or free energy (Joffily & Coricelli, 2013; Seth & Friston, 2016).
text.formatted: A related proposal links emotional valence to changes in prediction error or free energy <ref type="bibr">(Joffily & Coricelli, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seth & Friston, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In this view, improving predictions and resolving uncertainty can contribute to positive affect, whereas worsening prediction can contribute to negative affect.
These proposals concern the dynamics of inference, not a universal identification of any prediction-error decrease with physiological benefit.
Body-budget and hi-erarchical regulation accounts likewise connect preferences and motivated behavior to anticipated bodily demands (Barrett, 2017a; Pezzulo et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Body-budget and hi-erarchical regulation accounts likewise connect preferences and motivated behavior to anticipated bodily demands <ref type="bibr">(Barrett, 2017a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pezzulo et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Computational work makes aspects of this connection executable.

Yoshida and colleagues model internal physiological variables and drives that shape reinforcement signals and policy learning, allowing agents to acquire behaviors that restore physiological balance (Yoshida et al., 2024 (Yoshida et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Yoshida and colleagues model internal physiological variables and drives that shape reinforcement signals and policy learning, allowing agents to acquire behaviors that restore physiological balance <ref type="bibr">(Yoshida et al., 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Yoshida et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Idei and collaborators connect homeostatic regulation with inference in hierarchical neurorobotic and Bayesian models, examining how bodily and environmental uncertainty influence action (Idei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Idei and collaborators connect homeostatic regulation with inference in hierarchical neurorobotic and Bayesian models, examining how bodily and environmental uncertainty influence action <ref type="bibr">(Idei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These models provide mechanisms to investigate, rather than establishing a complete account of human emotion.
A glucose-regulation example distinguishes the questions involved.
Falling glucose can motivate anticipation of a future deficit and food-seeking.

HRL asks how reducing a bodily deviation rewards learning such behavior; predictive accounts ask how evidence and expectations about bodily change shape inference and action; valence proposals add the temporal dynamics of prediction error.
These objectives are connected but not interchangeable without model-specific assumptions, such as the cost and regularization assumptions under which Supplementary Section S2 compares HRL.
For TCoE, HRL contributes a bodily basis for evaluating action; how that evaluation couples to socially negotiated symbols is a further modeling question.
Social interaction can influence emotional experience and bodily regulation.
Parkinson's relationalignment account describes how emotions organize convergence, complementarity, or conflict between people's orientations to shared objects (Parkinson, 2021).
text.formatted: Parkinson's relationalignment account describes how emotions organize convergence, complementarity, or conflict between people's orientations to shared objects <ref type="bibr">(Parkinson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: TCoE asks how this relational process could be connected to private bodily evidence and communicable symbols, rather than assuming that interpersonal alignment requires identical internal states.
Social Baseline Theory treats proximity to others as a resource affecting estimates of risk and effort (Beckes & Coan, 2011; Coan & Sbarra, 2015).
text.formatted: Social Baseline Theory treats proximity to others as a resource affecting estimates of risk and effort <ref type="bibr">(Beckes & Coan, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Coan & Sbarra, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Reduced threat-related neural responses during spousal handholding illustrate how social relationships can modify responses to challenge (Coan et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Reduced threat-related neural responses during spousal handholding illustrate how social relationships can modify responses to challenge <ref type="bibr">(Coan et al., 2006)</ref>.

The proposed cycle has three stages.
First, individuals infer their bodily situation from private sensations and accessible context.

Alexithymia is a common personality trait characterized by difficulty expressing one's emotions in words.

Here, we reinterpret alexithymia not merely as altered emotional awareness, but as a disruption of the co-constructive process through which bodily states and social symbols are dynamically coupled to generate emotion.

In TCoE, language and emotion words are not mere labels but socially shared symbols that integrate heterogeneous interoceptive signals, exteroceptive context, and subjective evaluations into meaningful emotion concepts.
Such symbols help segment bodily fluctuations into patterns that guide judgment and regulation and align predictions within a linguistic community.
Alexithymia is clinically relevant precisely because this coupling between bodily inference and social symbols is thought to break down.

Recall from Section 4.4 that the latent internal state z represents bodily conditions, accessed only indirectly through interoceptive observations x int (e.g., cardiac sensations, visceral feelings), while q(z | x int ) denotes the posterior estimate of that state and shared emotion concepts w guide its interpretation.

In typical emotional experience, the posterior belief q(z | x int ) is stably formed from interoceptive observations, and the social symbol w provides a frame for interpreting it: words such as "anxiety" or "anger" predict bodily patterns and guide how those states are understood and regulated.

In alexithymia, however, low interoceptive precision can leave the posterior belief q(z | x int ) weakly constrained by bodily evidence: bodily states are experienced in a vague and undifferentiated manner, making it difficult to interpret them by reference to the social symbol w.
As a result, the social symbol fails to ground emotion word acceptance or revision, and the coordination between bodily interpretation and social meaning-making breaks down.
This coupling failure propagates upward.

When q(z | x int ) is unreliable, top-down social allostatic constraints cannot effectively regulate bodily states, and bodily signals that remain uncategorized persist as poorly resolved inputs, impeding free-energy minimization.
The resulting chronic mismatch between bodily states and social expectations may give rise to the psychosomatic symptoms frequently reported in alexithymia.
Empirical evidence supports this account of failed coupling at the level of bodily representations.
The disconnection between interoceptive signals and social symbols becomes most pronounced at the stage of mapping bodily states onto emotion concepts.

This predicts reduced bodily grounding of negotiation under those assumptions, rather than indiscriminate acceptance as a general consequence of low interoceptive precision.
The latent-state formulation remains an alternative, with acceptance evaluated at that level as described in Section 4.3.

This subsection examines the complementary failure in the recognition direction-inferring an appropriate emotion word from one's own bodily evidence-and reviews empirical support for the underlying interoceptive imprecision.

If emotion words and interoceptive sensations are interconnected in this manner, dysfunctions in interoceptive processing or in the formation of emotion concepts are likely to produce discrepancies between predicted and actual internal states.

Such discrepancies have been reported across a range of psychiatric conditions (Khalsa et al., 2018) and can be conceptualized here as a failure to connect with the collective predictive processes underlying emotional co-construction.

Rather, it reflects a vicious cycle in which imprecise interoceptive input and impoverished symbolic abstraction mutually reinforce one another, resulting in a breakdown of the co-constructive coupling between interoceptive inference and social symbolic systems that gives rise to emotion in TCoE.

This distinction is empirically testable: manipulating interoceptive precision should change emotion-word acceptance even with label input held constant, whereas the label-ambiguity account predicts stronger sensitivity to linguisticfeedback consistency.
The flattening of the marginal likelihood described in Section 5.1 also affects recognition: inferring an emotion word from one's own bodily evidence.
By Bayes' rule, the posterior over words depends on their marginal likelihoods and prior probabilities (Supplementary Section S5.3).
When the likelihood is word-invariant, the posterior reduces to the prior.
Bodily evidence then no longer distinguishes among words, but their probabilities need not be equal unless the prior is uniform.

text.text: Thus, impaired bodily grounding affects both acceptance during social negotiation and recognition in self-labeling.
This computational account also suggests a principled basis for therapeutic interventions.

Strategies that target interoceptive precision (bottom-up, e.g., heartbeat discrimination training, Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA)-based body-state calibration) and strategies that target emotion vocabulary restructuring (top-down, e.g., guided re-labeling, context-rich emotional socialization) can both be understood as restoring the coupling between bodily evidence and emotion words in the acceptance and recognition directions formalized above.
The framework predicts that integrated interventions addressing both sides simultaneously should be more effective than either alone.
At the same time, alexithymia is heterogeneous, and interoceptive precision alone cannot account for all clinical manifestations.
Attention, working memory, developmental history, interpersonal experience, and culture can modulate bodily inference and emotion-word use.
Quantitative links between model precision and behavioral measures, such as heartbeat-matching tolerance and physiological-subjective discordance, remain to be established.
TCoE therefore provides a promising computational re-description rather than a complete clinical account.
First, following the acceptance dynamics formalized in Section 5.1, TCoE predicts an asymmetry in lexical dominance within dyads that differ in interoceptive precision.
When a highprecision individual and a low-precision individual interact repeatedly, the shared emotion vocabulary should converge toward the high-precision individual's word usage.
The proposed mechanism is reduced bodily selectivity on one side and stronger bodily grounding on the other.

In the matched observation-level MHNG formulation, approximately word-invariant listener likelihoods make acceptance approach unity (Supplementary Section S5.2), whereas informative likelihoods allow more selective evaluation.
This asymmetric convergence is a prediction that no purely individual-level theory can generate.

It also connects to development: mothers' understanding of emotion-interoception links is associated with children's emotion regulation (MacCormack et al., 2020), and emotion-concept acquisition requires categorizing bodily and contextual experiences (Hoemann et al., 2020).

text.text: TCoE frames this acquisition as MHNG-like interaction coupling shared symbols with bodily inference.

Second, as testable predictions about repeated interaction, TCoE proposes that the rate of convergence of emotion vocabularies should depend on the interoceptive precision of both participants: high-precision dyads converge rapidly to body-grounded labels; low-precision dyads converge but to prior-driven labels with lower cross-dyad consistency; mixed dyads show intermediate speed with strong asymmetry in who drives the final vocabulary.

These predictions can be tested in controlled experiments where pairs interact over emotion-labeling tasks, with interoceptive precision measured independently (e.g., heartbeat discrimination accuracy).

Symmetric convergence regardless of interoceptive precision, or convergence explained by social dominance or linguistic fluency rather than bodily-state coupling, would require revision of the current formulation.
The strongest test is whether precision predicts asymmetric convergence after controlling for dominance, verbal ability, and prior label familiarity.
Similarly, a lack of greater bodily selectivity in high-precision individuals would challenge the proposed marginallikelihood mechanism.
These boundary conditions distinguish TCoE from competing accounts.

In typical development, TCoE reframes emotion-word acquisition as a co-constructive process in which children and caregivers iteratively align bodily experience and shared symbols, rather than passively internalizing labels.

The target is the neural implementation of this comparison process, not merely activation in interoceptive or semantic regions.

Three predictions follow.

First, when multiple agents equipped with interoceptive generative models engage in MHNG-style symbol negotiation, a shared emotion vocabulary should self-organize without pre-specifying fixed categories.

Third, varying interaction topology or partner assignment should systematically shift the boundaries of emergent emotion categories, demonstrating that category structure is a function of collective dynamics rather than individual embodiment alone.
Constructive validation cannot rest on simulation alone.

Ultimately, it is necessary to test, using real parent-child interaction data, how social interaction connects children's interoceptive states, behavioral expressions, and the formation of emotion words.

Feldman's research has shown that parent-infant synchrony and children's emotion regulation mutually predict each other across development (2012)-a bidirectional, temporally structured dynamic that is precisely what TCoE's allostatic and social loops predict.

Datasets of parent-child physiological synchrony (Bizzego et al., 2022; Capraz et al., 2023; Tamis-LeMonda, 2023) and reports of partner-specific differences in synchrony between mother-child and father-child dyads (Puglisi et al., 2023) offer rich targets for validating how social allostatic priors and dyadic coordination are established in actual developmental processes.

text.text: The deepest frontier lies at the intersection of these two directions: building robots with genuine homeostatic needs-systems whose continued operation depends on managing a real body budget-would introduce the physical constraints of embodied interoception into the social dynamics of collective symbol emergence via CPC.
Under such dual constraints, where neither the body nor the social relationship is simulated, one can ask whether something struc-turally analogous to human emotion-concept formation emerges.

If it does, this would constitute the strongest constructive evidence for Barrett's claim that the brain evolved primarily as a body-budget manager, and for TCoE's claim that this management is irreducibly social.
The intersection of bodily and social constraint is, in this sense, where the constructive study of emotion becomes the constructive study of mind.
A related future direction is to extend HRL beyond individual homeostatic regulation toward collective body-budget management in social interaction.

Such an extension would require augmenting individual homeostatic cost with social-allostatic and collective-symbolic terms, so that policies are evaluated not only by their effects on one's own bodily prediction errors but also by their contribution to alignment with shared emotion symbols and collective coordination.
We leave this formal development for future work.

The central contribution of this article is to show that emotion is neither confined to the individual body nor imposed on the individual by society, but co-constructed in the cycle between interoceptive prediction and social symbol sharing.

Grounded in CPC, TCoE connects the individual loop of interoceptive inference and predictive adjustment with the social loop of sharing and updating emotion words and concepts under a single principle of free energy minimization, bridging psychological and social constructivism within one formal framework.

The key role of CPC is to treat the shared symbol w not as a fixed external condition but as a latent variable updated through collective interaction, thereby representing both how society shapes individuals and how their interactions transform shared emotional concepts.
In sum, TCoE extends the computational understanding of emotion from something made inside the body to something co-constructed between body and society.

CPC formalizes this process through the dynamics of prediction and symbol generation, with implications for alexithymia, emotion formation and vocabulary development, and social simulation using artificial agents.

The essence of emotion lies not in private experience enclosed within the individual, nor in fixed categories given by society, but in a co-constructive process that is continually rewoven in the reciprocal movement between bodily prediction and social symbols.
This proposal is the first to describe this process systematically as a computational theory.
Several important scope conditions of TCoE should be noted.
As a computational-level theory, TCoE specifies what is computed during emotion co-construction.
Its neural implementation remains an open question: which brain regions support interoceptive precision weighting, emotion-word marginal likelihood computation, or the MHNG acceptance decision?
The neuroscientific research program outlined above addresses this question.

The current formulation also treats model parameters as stationary within each interaction episode, abstracts away from attention, working memory, and executive control, and does not yet accommodate social emotions such as shame, guilt, and jealousy, which presuppose recursive social comparison beyond the single shared symbol w.

This single-symbol assumption is a simplifying entry point rather than a principled limit of CPC: the same framework can in principle be extended to hierarchical or simultaneous systems of shared symbols.

text.text: Specifically, shared symbols (e.g., the word "anxiety") act as priors for expected bodily states within a group.
Individual agents attempt to resolve the mismatch (prediction error) arising between these socially shared symbols and their own interoceptive sensations.
Consequently, through the sharing of symbols, even individual physiological states (allostasis) are socially modulated and aligned.
Conversely, these symbols are originally formed to symbolically express and share the somatic experiences felt by each individual.

In essence, emotional co-construction is a dynamic process in which the individual interoceptive loop (body regulation) and the social symbolic loop (communication) mutually constrain each other, allowing the collective whole to mutually regulate emotional states.

This decomposition highlights two distinct forces driving the individual agent, mirroring the structure of the individual terms in CPC: • Prediction Error (Negative Accuracy): The first term drives the agent to explain the current interoceptive observation x int t using its internal state estimate z t .
Minimizing this term corresponds to maximizing the sensory likelihood.
• Regularization (Complexity): The second term penalizes the divergence between the posterior belief and the top-down prior p(z t | w t ).
Because the prior is conditioned on the emotion word w t , this term constrains the posterior belief by the word-conditioned expectation.

The important point for TCoE is not the particular sensory implementation, but the role of selective acceptance and rejection: indiscriminate acceptance of proposed signs is insufficient, whereas selective negotiation can form a shared symbolic scaffold over non-identical bodily representations, allowing category alignment without requiring agents to converge on identical internal states.
Tsubamoto and Horii (2026) shift the focus from category alignment to homeostatic co-regulation.

Their mother-infant model represents an asymmetric POMDP setting in which the parent agent has a regulatory model for maintaining the infant's body budget but must infer the infant's state from external cues, whereas the infant has direct interoceptive access to its own visceral state but must learn which coordinated actions maintain homeostasis.

MHNG-style communication lets the two agents negotiate shared symbols on the basis of their own state estimates, and shared representation can emerge before the agents' generative model parameters fully converge.

From the perspective of TCoE, this illustrates how a social symbolic loop may become coupled to an individual allostatic loop: communication does not merely transmit labels, but can help coordinate physiological regulation across agents with different access to bodily information.
Building on this homeostatic co-regulation setting, Nomura et al. (2026) address how the meaning of shared symbols may itself emerge and change through interaction.

This provides a constructive approximation to a further TCoE claim: emotion-like symbols are not fixed labels attached to bodily states, but renegotiated meanings whose interpretants can coevolve with agents' allostatic histories.
Taken together, these studies do not yet constitute a full realization of the TCoE objective.

Instead, they clarify three constructive tasks implied by the framework: aligning emotion categories across non-identical bodies, coupling symbolic communication to social allostatic regulation, and allowing symbol meaning itself to evolve through interaction.
Because these studies remain preliminary and largely pre-publication, they should be treated as engineering testbeds rather than conclusive demonstrations.

The activation of these neurons by DREADD is consistent with a prediction-error account: artificially reactivating inflammation-related predictions could trigger bodily activation in the form of inflammation to reduce the prediction error.

Homeostatic Reinforcement Learning (HRL) is a normative theory that grounds the source of motivation, namely reward signals, in the internal dynamics of the body by defining rewards as reductions in deviations from physiologically desirable states (set points) (Hulme et al., 2019; Keramati & Gutkin, 2014; Pezzulo et al., 2015).

text.text: It specifically addresses reinforcement learning problems in which the maintenance of homeostasis is the central regulatory objective, grounding motivational signals in reductions of physiological deviations rather than identifying them with sensory prediction error.
Relatedly, Seth and Friston (2016) argued that emotion can be understood as the temporal change in free energy, or prediction error.
text.formatted: Relatedly, <ref type="bibr">Seth and Friston (2016)</ref> argued that emotion can be understood as the temporal change in free energy, or prediction error.

text.text: They stated that pleasant emotions arise when the model updates in a direction that reduces prediction error, while unpleasant emotions occur when uncertainty increases.
This idea is developed in Joffily and Coricelli's (2013) mathematical model, which hypothesizes that emotional valence corresponds to the sign of prediction-error dynamics.
For example, considering fluctuations in blood glucose levels-a crucial interoceptive sensory event-the brain predicts the onset of hypoglycemia when glucose is decreasing.
The discrepancy between this prediction and the actual physical state is encoded as a prediction error.
As the error increases, eating behavior is prompted.

At this point, the subjective experience of hunger is not merely a reflection of physiological state but the subjective experience of a prediction-error signal indicating that the predictive model should be revised (Joffily & Coricelli, 2013; Seth & Friston, 2016).

text.text: Predictive accounts complement the physiological-deviation objective of HRL by considering expectations about future bodily changes and the temporal dynamics of inference.

These quantities are related but are not interchangeable definitions of reward. text.text: Metabolic state can influence decision-making and value judgments, with energy-rich foods-options excellent for short-term energy replenishment-being more likely to be chosen under stress or homeostatic load.
This occurs because when the body budget is strained, the predictive model updates to highly value choices that rapidly replenish energy.
Together, HRL and active-inference accounts provide a framework for connecting emotion, value, and decision-making to bodily regulation.
Their objectives can be related under explicit modeling assumptions, but reducing sensory prediction error does not by itself guarantee physiological benefit.

From this perspective, the ability to more accurately predict the body's in-ternal states and minimize bodily prediction errors can drive motivated behavior (Hulme et al., 2019; Keramati & Gutkin, 2014; Pezzulo et al., 2018).

text.text: This perspective transcends traditional models centered on external rewards and provides a crucial framework for clarifying the computational basis of emotions.
Recent work has begun to implement these theoretical ideas in neurally grounded computational models of homeostatic regulation.

Yoshida and colleagues developed a computational framework of homeostatically regulated reinforcement learning in which internal physiological variables are explicitly represented as latent states that shape reward prediction and policy learning.
In their formulation, deviations from physiological set points generate internal drives that modulate reinforcement signals, enabling agents to learn behaviors that restore physiological balance.

Simulation studies demonstrated that such agents can acquire adaptive policies-such as food-seeking or energy-conserving behaviors-through learning processes that directly incorporate internal bodily states into the value function (Yoshida et al., 2024 (Yoshida et al., , 2025)).

text.text: These results provide a mechanistic account of how homeostatic variables can serve as the internal basis of value and motivation within reinforcement learning architectures.
Complementary work by Idei and collaborators further integrates HRL with predictive coding.

Using neurorobotic and Bayesian network models based on hierarchical generative architectures, they showed that agents can simultaneously infer external environmental states and internal bodily states while minimizing prediction errors across these domains.
In these models, homeostatic regulation emerges from the dynamic interaction between action selection and the inference of interoceptive signals.

Importantly, their simulations demonstrated that exploratory behaviors, context-sensitive decisionmaking, and mode switching between goal-directed and sensory-focused behavior can arise spontaneously as agents attempt to maintain stable internal states under uncertain environmental conditions (Idei et al., 2025).

This argument also clarifies why language is central to collective emotion construction. Barrett and Miller (2026) argue that categorization is not a late stage added after perception, but a core predictive operation embedded throughout neural signal processing.

In social interaction, language therefore does more than report pre-existing emotions; it helps align the categories through which interoceptive prediction errors are inter-preted and shared.

text.text: This section provides further detail on the constructive models reviewed in the main article, including their architectures, findings, and implications for the body-symbol cycle proposed by TCoE.

The robotics studies reviewed below illustrate how constructive approaches provide a synthetic method for studying emotional dynamics that are too complex to be fully understood through observation and analysis alone.

Because emotion unfolds through closed loops among bodily regulation, action, interaction, and symbolic interpretation, it is crucial to build embodied systems in which these loops can be instantiated and tested.

Robotics offers such a platform: constructing agents that regulate, express, and acquire emotion-like states makes it possible to examine how emotional processes may emerge from bodily and social dynamics.

Historically, however, early research on affective robotics predominantly relied on pattern recognition models that extracted emotion categories from facial expressions, vocal features, or discrete physiological signals (Breazeal, 2003; Picard, 1997).
text.formatted: Historically, however, early research on affective robotics predominantly relied on pattern recognition models that extracted emotion categories from facial expressions, vocal features, or discrete physiological signals <ref type="bibr">(Breazeal, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Picard, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Representative systems in this tradition treated emotion as a fixed mapping from external stimuli to categorical outputs-valuable for human-robot interaction in controlled settings, but fundamentally limited: the agent's internal bodily state played no generative role in emotional processing, and the question of how emotion categories themselves come to be was never posed.
Cognitive developmental robotics (Asada et al., 2001 (Asada et al., , 2009;; Pfeifer & Bongard, 2006) offers a different starting point.
text.formatted: Cognitive developmental robotics <ref type="bibr">(Asada et al., 2001</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Asada et al., , 2009;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pfeifer & Bongard, 2006)</ref> offers a different starting point.

text.text: Rather than pre-defining emotional categories and training a classifier to detect them, it asks how a robot-through autonomous sensorimotor interaction with its environment and others-can self-organize the concept of emotion from the ground up.

This approach has developed in parallel with the theoretical frameworks reviewed in Section 2 of the main article, and provides a means to test their computational claims in physically embodied sys-tems.

S4.3 The Need for Co-constructed Emotion Despite these advances, a fundamental limitation is shared across all state-of-the-art single-agent emotion models: the question of where the social prior distribution comes from in the first place remains unanswered.

Even in the experiments by Smith et al., learning the observation matrix that maps latent states to observable cues relies heavily on top-down labeling by caregivers alongside environmental interaction.

This dependency is not merely a modeling convenience: Atzil et al. (2018) demonstrate that caregiver-infant interaction shapes the developing allostatic and social brain at a structural level, with caregivers serving as the external allostatic scaffolding through which the infant's physiological regulation and emotion category formation are co-constituted.

A single-agent model, by treating caregiver input as a fixed environmental variable, cannot represent this constitutively social character of emotion development-the prior does not merely come "from outside" but is itself generated through a developmentally embedded allostatic relationship.

The grounding of the acquired latent variables' meanings and the boundaries of their interpretation depend on fixed environmental structures or external others, failing to account for the long-term dynamics of how emotion concepts transform within society.
In other words, the prior is treated as given-precisely the theoretical gap identified in Section 1 of the main article with respect to social constructivism.
This limitation points to a developmental reality: emotion concepts do not arise in isolation but are shaped from the earliest stages of life through social interaction.

The key computational question, therefore, is how a group of agents-each with its own interoceptive generative model-can come to share emotion concepts through interaction, rather than having those concepts imposed from outside.
Section 4 of the main article formalizes this problem as TCoE via CPC.

TCoE generates empirical predictions that are distinct from those of individual-level constructivist theories of emotion because it is explicitly a theory of dyadic co-construction.

The central predictions concern not merely the relationship between interoception and emotion labeling within a single individual, but the dynamics of emotion word convergence through iterated social interaction.

p(x int | w) should correspond to neural processes that evaluate the compatibility between bodily state and an emotion word; the prior p(w) should correspond to socially and linguistically acquired expectations over available labels; the acceptance computation should correspond to neural mechanisms that compare a newly proposed word with the current shared state; and precision weighting should correspond to the modulation of how strongly interoceptive evidence constrains that comparison.
Although the precise neural substrates remain open, TCoE predicts that these components cannot be fully understood within single-agent paradigms alone.
The most direct neuroscientific tests should use interactive paradigms in which one participant proposes an emotion word and another accepts or rejects it during neural recording.
Supporting evidence would include responses modulated jointly by bodily state and shared lexical context, with individual differences related to interoceptive precision.
